To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the pain experience of hospice cancer patients is complex.

elderly patients with cancer receiving hospice care experience multiple sites of pain, which are differentiated by the participants into physical and psychological pain; the physical pain is described as a hierarchy, with acute pain being the worst; pharmacological and nonpharmalogical strategies are used to decrease physical pain, but the participants perceive that there is little they can do about their psychological pain.

elderly patients with cancer who are receiving hospice services experience pain at multiple sites, describe their pain as being hierarchical, and use both pharmacological and nonpharmaceutical strategies to decrease pain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pain experience of hospice cancer patients.
the pain experiences of hospice patients with terminal cancer.
the pain experience of the elderly hospice patient with cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the pain experience of the elderly hospice patient with cancer is complex, multidimensional, and multifaceted.

the elderly cancer patient with pain experiences a hierarchy of pain that includes physical pain, chronic pain, acute pain, and psychological pain; and uses pharmacological and nonpharmalogical strategies to decrease pain.
elderly hospice cancer patients experience a complex and multidimensional pain experience.

pain is a complex experience, and it is important to understand the multiple sites, hierarchy, and strategies of pain to provide the most effective pain relief.
elderly cancer patients with chronic pain are at high risk for developing a hierarchy of pain that is difficult to treat.
elderly hospice cancer patients have a complex pain experience that requires a comprehensive approach for treatment.

pain is a complex experience, which can be described in different ways.
